courses.name: Directed Study
courses.subject: SCHM
courses.description: Offers independent work under the direction of members of the department on chosen topics. May be repeated without limit.

courses.name: Sustainable Engineering Systems for Buildings
courses.subject: SBSY
courses.description: Focuses on the design and construction of sustainable mechanical/electrical/plumbing (MEP) systems in buildings. Covers MEP documentation, plumbing water supply, HVAC systems, electrical power supply and distribution, lighting systems, low-voltage electrical systems, and estimating and planning for these specialty areas. Addresses sustainable design and construction practices for MEP, including minimization of energy consumption and carbon footprint. Requires one semester of building physics, environmental systems, or equivalent.

courses.name: Information Systems for Integrated Project Delivery
courses.subject: SBSY
courses.description: Focuses on new software systems for increasing efficiency of project delivery and facilitating design and construction integration through the use of BIM (Building Information Modeling) and related technologies. Exposes students to various software systems, including hands-on cases of BIM use, 4D (construction drawings linked to schedule) modeling, and 5D models (4D + cost). Covers the impact of new technology on project delivery, including owner’s perspective, advantages, and disadvantages. Also covers use and background of common industry systems to apply BIM concepts to construction projects.

courses.name: Sustainable Building Systems Seminar
courses.subject: SBSY
courses.description: Features prominent speakers from the sustainable building design and construction industry to showcase new building technologies, tools, and projects and to discuss national and international trends in the industry. Offers students an opportunity to meet innovators and key players advancing the field of sustainable building systems. May be repeated without limit.

courses.name: Deep Energy Retrofitting for Commercial Buildings
courses.subject: SBSY
courses.description: Explores deep energy retrofits of existing buildings to meet stringent energy performance targets and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Covers analysis, planning, design, implementation, and evaluation of retrofit interventions using building audits, sensing, forensic analysis, surveys, cost estimating, and simulation. Integrates students’ prior knowledge and experience in architectural engineering, building science, energy analysis, and economic decision making.

courses.name: Master's Project
courses.subject: SBSY
courses.description: Offers students an opportunity for individual participation in an advanced research project in an area of sustainable building systems engineering. Topic is determined by the student and their advisor. Students complete individual laboratory, literature, and/or computational investigation; analysis of results; and preparation of a definitive report.

courses.name: Master’s Research Studio: Master’s Project
courses.subject: SUEN
courses.description: Constitutes the second half of the Master’s Research Studio sequence. Using the design thesis established in SUEN 7130, offers students an opportunity to formulate proposals for intervention into a specific urbanized environment. Individual projects progress with instructor guidance from schematic phasing through design development, with a focus on change management and vitalization of the ecologic, economic, social, and aesthetic facets of contemporary cities and regions. Requires individual presentation and defense of master’s projects in written, oral, and digital formats. May be repeated once.

courses.name: Urban Ecologies and Technologies 2
courses.subject: SUEN
courses.description: Offers a community outreach course as the second in a two-part sequence and builds upon SUEN 7230. The core theme is development of innovative, market-based ecotechnology prototypes for the urban landscape that contribute to the environmental and cultural life of the city. With instructor guidance, offers students an opportunity to identify a potential ecotechnology project to design through engagement with community members, public, or institutional clients. The course outcome includes site documentation; a schematic design proposal produced by students working in groups; and, if appropriate in terms of time, budget, and scale, implementation.

courses.name: Pro-Seminar: Issues in Designed Urban Environments
courses.subject: SUEN
courses.description: Offers an advanced graduate seminar examining the forces shaping designed urban environments in contemporary global culture. A diverse range of material from published design criticism to open source social media engagement provides basis for discussion and written and oral presentations. Course themes determined by the instructor parallel the studio sequence SUEN 7130 and SUEN 7140, although discussion topics are broadly presented to engage graduate students from any background. May be repeated up to three times.

courses.name: Writing for the Web
courses.subject: TCC
courses.description: Compares and contrasts how readers/viewers scan rather than read Web pages and why Web writing differs from traditional text/prose writing. Describes writing styles and how to structure information for the Web. Defines human factors and how they affect writing for the Web. Describes Web navigation and labeling, examines visualization concepts and theory, and presents the processes of evaluation and usability testing. This writing-intensive course offers students an opportunity both for hands-on laboratory-type experiences through planning, designing, building, and testing Web sites and for collaborative work with classmates.

courses.name: Technology Leadership 2
courses.subject: TELR
courses.description: Continues the examination of technology practices begun in TELR 5121. Requires work/training with a sponsoring organization or employer to improve a process or develop a project that is of significant value to the organization and demonstrates a quantifiable market impact while enhancing the student’s technological depth and fostering the student’s leadership development.

courses.name: Scientific Foundations of Technology 2
courses.subject: TELR
courses.description: Continues the examination of fundamental science begun in TELR 5131.

courses.name: Technology Leadership Challenge Project 2
courses.subject: TELR
courses.description: Continues TELR 7440, a thesis-scale project in technology commercialization. Offers students an opportunity to demonstrate their development of a marketable technology product or prototype and to produce a written documentary report on the project to the satisfaction of an advising committee. Requires work/training with a sponsoring organization or employer to improve a process or develop a project that is of significant value to the organization and demonstrates a quantifiable market impact while enhancing the student’s technological depth and fostering the student’s leadership development.

courses.name: Data Networking
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Provides the basics of data networking protocols and architectures. Topics include protocol architecture of the internet; application protocols such as FTP, SMTP and HTTP, web caching, DNS, CDNs, and P2P applications; use of TCP and UDP socket programming to develop network applications in Python; transport protocols, including TCP, UDP, and TCP congestion control; IP protocol, addressing, IPv4 and v6, NATs, ICMP, and tunnels; routing algorithms and OSPF; data link protocols, encoding, framing, error control, and PPP; switched LANs, ARP, Ethernet, and VLANs; wireless LANs and 802.11 protocols; and network security—encryption, message integrity, authentication protocols, key management, SSL/TLS, IPsec, and 802.11i.

courses.name: Lab for TELE 5330
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Addresses a range of networking components, including routers, switches, and Linux servers, and how they are configured to create a virtual environment. Covers the installation and configuration of networking concepts such as DNS, DHCP, and firewalls and the creation of virtual environments. Requires students, working in teams, to configure one or more components; the teams then must interconnect the components to form a small network. In the process of configuration and integration, students are exposed to troubleshooting at various protocol layers and have an opportunity to become familiarized with different operating systems and networking tools.

courses.name: Telecom and Network Infrastructure
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Provides in-depth treatment of the wireline and wireless infrastructure of the network supporting all telecommunication, internet, and enterprise applications. Covers the basics of communications—source coding, baseband and broadband modulation and transmission, channel coding, spread-spectrum, multiuser radio communications, radio link analysis, and propagation. Also covers the wireline core network—digital and optical transmission, framing, network synchronization, asynchronous and synchronous multiplexing, cross connects, SONET/SDH, DWDM, OTN, protection switching, and network availability. Addresses wireline (DSL, digital cable, FTTx, PONs) and wireless access (cellular, Wi-Fi), frequency reuse, and handoff. Also addresses support of data transport (switched Ethernet, VLAN, IP, MPLS) and application networks (PSTN, mobile core, internet, IPTV, and virtual networks).

courses.name: Internet Protocols and Architecture
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Offers in-depth treatment of protocols used in the internet, wireless access, and enterprise networks. Topics include protocols for network layer QoS (including DiffServ, ECN, RSVP, MPLS); protocols for security, including both access control and network-level security (e.g., X.509, SSL/TLS, IPsec, IKE, EAP); protocols for interdomain routing (BGP); protocols to support multicast, broadcast, and streaming applications; protocols to support host mobility, large server deployments, content distribution, and enterprise networks (VLANs, etc); and protocols to support IPv6 (e.g., address assignment) and its interoperability with IPv4. Also covers network design architectures for cloud computing, data centers, content distribution, layer-2 networks, etc. Discusses general scaling issues for large networks.

courses.name: Linux/UNIX Systems Management for Network Engineers
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Introduces UNIX/Linux in a networking/Internet environment. Covers operating system concepts, tools, and utilities; networking and security issues; and data and text processing using scripts and filters. Addresses basic administrative tasks such as managing users, file systems, security, and software. Covers networking topics such as network configuration, daemon processes, SSH, DNS, DHCP, diagnostic tools, and the use of scripts and automation to manage applications and systems, as well as security topics such as name and authentication services, access control lists, file modification protections, and firewalls.

courses.name: Communication and Network Security
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Studies the skills necessary to apply and implement network and communication security in enterprise environments. Covers various concepts related to computer security and network protection. Explores systems security, access control, network infrastructure, assessments and audits, cryptography, and organizational security, all of which help to protect enterprise networks' confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Covers common network attacks, cryptography basics, computer forensics, and operational/organizational security related to physical security, disaster recovery, and business continuity. Discusses recent trends in network security attacks and cyberattacks, analyzing worms and trojans, SSL/TLS session renegotiations/compression, DNS security, spam, and crypto-based countermeasures.

courses.name: Infrastructure Automation Design and Tools
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Exposes students to best practices for infrastructure automation, which is highly critical in the design and deployment of network and server infrastructure that supports microservices architecture applications on public cloud (IaaS) services. Provides hands-on experience with IaC (infrastructure as code) technologies for provisioning and deprovisioning, configuration, patching, security, monitoring, alerting, logging, etc., for infrastructure components ranging from network devices to servers to entire virtual data centers. Focuses on both individual and team projects involving the use of IaC tools such as Ansible, Puppet, Git, Selenium, Netmiko, Paramiko, CFEngine, Docker, and Kubernetes for infrastructure deployment and automation.

courses.name: Machine Learning for IoT Systems
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Studies the design, development, rollout, and maintenance of machine learning algorithms for IoT systems, which generate and process time series data under memory and timeliness constraints. Focuses on verticals like Industry 4.0, wearables, and smart grids/homes. Explores the nuances of handling IoT time series data in both edge and cloud computing settings including the preparation, exploration, and feature engineering for sensor data. Covers domain-specific problem classes like forecasting, change point detection, and temporal anomaly detection. Addresses customized performance metrics for time series algorithms. Analyzes deep learning architectures for time series problems using TinyML for embedded devices. Course projects focus on time series, going beyond traditional datasets used in conventional ML classes.

courses.name: Fundamentals of the Internet of Things
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Explores the foundations of and technologies involved in the Internet of Things (IoT). Topics include machine-to-machine (M2M) communications and its relationship with IoT. Examines fundamental components of the IoT architecture reviewing industry standards. Presents a large array of case studies. Discusses the fundamentals of data networks with a focus on different wireless technologies relevant to IoT, including the latest developments in IEEE 802.11, IEEE 802.15.4, and BLE, as well as network layer protocols such as 6LoWPAN that are critical to the deployment of wireless IoT networks. Discusses a range of IoT application protocols, especially MQTT, CoAP, and AMQP. Also explores IoT security and privacy considerations and identification mechanisms for IoT devices. Introduces wireless sensor networks and routing protocols for wireless networks.

courses.name: Connected Devices
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Offers an in-depth, software-intensive exploration of the Internet of Things (IoT)—from device to cloud—culminating in a semester-long project where each student designs, builds, and presents an end-to-end, integrated IoT solution. Covers IoT concepts and architectures, and incorporates significant software development activities through weekly modules. Includes testing, DevOps, and messaging protocols specific to the IoT; device integration; and cloud services designed for IoT ecosystems.

courses.name: IoT Embedded System Design
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Explores the technologies and techniques behind the field of design and development of modern embedded devices in IoT systems. Specifically, focuses on a hands-on approach to software development on an embedded hardware platform. Through a final project, students have an opportunity to build and deploy an industrial-grade state-of-the-art embedded IoT solution. Presents C coding, but also reviews the ARM ISA as well as C++ development and debugging. Applies theoretical concepts to practical issues including pipelining, parallelism, concurrency, memory architectures, and I/O (GPIO, I2C, UART, SPI). Introduces bare-metal and OS-based development focusing on multitasking, scheduling, interrupts, threads, processes, tasks, IPC, drivers, contention resolution, and shared memory. Introduces state-of-the-art Google Cloud IoT and FreeRTOS APIs.

courses.name: Special Topics in the Internet of Things
courses.subject: TELE

courses.name: Master's Project
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Supports a project in cyber-physical systems and the Internet of Things that may have both hardware and software elements. Project to be carried out under faculty supervision.

courses.name: Thesis
courses.subject: TELE
courses.description: Offers students an opportunity to conduct theoretical and experimental work under the supervision of a departmental faculty.

courses.name: Theatre at Northeastern
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description:
Introduces new students to the communities and procedures of Northeastern University; the College of Arts, Media and Design; and the Department of Theatre. Offers insights into the study of the liberal arts in general and the creative facets of theatre study, including the rehearsal and production process. Emphasizes the departmental values of generosity, respect, and rigor and seeks to familiarize students with the arts and culture of Greater Boston.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Ryder 440

courses.name: Production Experience 1
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Offers lab practice in technical production. May be repeated once.

courses.name: Introduction to Theatre
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Reveals the dynamic world of theatre by exploring the artistry, ideas, and techniques of actors, designers, directors, and playwrights. Goes behind the scenes in the study of theory and literature with both in-depth discussions and in-class performances. Includes a survey of significant movements in theatre history and analysis of diverse plays from contemporary drama. No theatre experience required.

courses.name: Improvisation
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Introduces theatre improvisation principles through games, exercises, and readings. Offers a playful and rigorous environment for students to respond to unexpected situations with confidence and agility. In this experiential studio course, students participate in group and individual exercises that explore and practice creative impulses, adaptability, risk taking, intuition, and teamwork. Culminates in a self-reflection paper.

courses.name: Introduction to Acting
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Introduces techniques that awaken the creative mind, body, and spirit of the actor. Through theatre games and voice/movement exercises, offers students an opportunity to explore and develop skills used by actors in preparation for a role. Students rehearse and perform scenes from contemporary plays. Designed for nontheatre majors; previous stage experience welcome but not required.

courses.name: Introduction to Technical Theatre
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Surveys the technical and stagecraft skills that are essential knowledge for all theatre professionals. Offers students an opportunity to develop a hands-on understanding of the areas of scenery and costume construction, stage management, props, and lighting. Covers the practical skills needed to participate in the creation, evaluation, and revision of a theatrical production. Coursework includes laboratory-based classes in the department scene shop and costume shop.

courses.name: The Evolution of Fashion and Costume
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Traces the evolution of fashion and costume as a global cultural phenomenon. Focuses on the history and meaning of clothing design and the development of style using a non-chronological approach. Fashion does not occur only in Western capitals; it has existed for centuries in every region of the world. Clothing has been used to protect our bodies, establish relationships with others, indicate our status, and express our identities. Through readings, discussions, research, writings, and presentations, offers an opportunity to discover the extraordinary power of fashion and clothing.

courses.name: Introduction to Global Fashion Studies: History, Theory, and Contemporary Practice
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Offers students an overview of the most significant and relevant theories on fashion, focusing on the cultural significance of clothing and style. Examines the intersection of fashion and other areas of study including the arts, history, economics, business, sociology, and anthropology. Explores global issues of gender, race, class, identity, image, style, material culture, and sustainability. Examines how populations from several postindustrial nations think about fashion, how globalization impacts their cultures and identities, and how designers and trendsetters are emerging from the new capitals of fashion.

courses.name: Introduction to Theatrical Design
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Introduces the principles of contemporary theatrical design and how to apply the creative process to scenery, costumes, and lighting. Offers students an opportunity to discover how design concepts are developed and relate to each other through research, script analysis, color theory, and visual composition. Seeks to develop the student’s capacity for collaboration and techniques for conceptualizing a play into a multidisciplinary work of art. No theatre experience required.

courses.name: Production Experience 2
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Offers lab practice in rehearsal and performance for production. May be repeated once.

courses.name: Playwriting
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Presents a collaborative workshop for developing authorial voice through creation of theatrical dialogue, scenes, and creative material. Analyzes contemporary plays, explores form and structure, and provides in-class writing prompts and workshopping of student work. Offers students an opportunity to write several short pieces, culminating in a one-act play.

courses.name: Acting for the Camera
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Explores the craft and methods used by actors while working in front of the camera through monologues, scenes, and group projects. Provides students with techniques to identify and free their performance energy with a foundation on relaxation and authenticity. Includes the study and analysis of acting styles in diverse genres of film and television from situation comedies to dramas. Offers students an opportunity to explore a range of on-camera skills and acting techniques and apply them in filmed final projects. Previous acting experience suggested but not required.

courses.name: Lighting Design
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Examines basic principles and practices of stage lighting, including the qualities and functions of light, lighting instruments and controls, use of color and directionality, and script analysis for lighting design elements. Offers students an opportunity to develop foundational skills and practice systematic reasoning in the programming and operation of lighting computer equipment. Through group projects and individual lab work, students create and execute lighting designs. Includes work on electrics crews for university productions.

courses.name: Fashion Construction and Pattern Making
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Offers students an opportunity to develop the skills and techniques necessary for creating and using basic master patterns and dress forms to create skirts, dresses, trousers, and tops. Covers basic fashion construction, flat patterning, draping, and finishing techniques.

courses.name: Rehearsal and Production
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Offers students an opportunity to develop the experimental skills associated with dramatic interpretation and theatrical production by working on Department of Theatre productions under the supervision of faculty and staff. Most students enrolled in this course engage in the practices associated with one of the following areas: acting, design, stage management, or production crew head. Fulfills the experiential education requirement for theatre majors. May be repeated three times.

courses.name: Capstone: Creative Practice Research Project
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Offers students an opportunity to conduct creative practice research, which is comprised of two components: the research, preparation, and execution of a substantial position of responsibility for a departmental production or a special creative practice project, under the supervision of a faculty member. Students write a capstone thesis paper, developing an original argument on a focused topic adjacent to their creative practice project. Students synthesize academic and experiential education through the paper, which requires research and analysis of focused evidence to make an original contribution to the current scholarly and/or professional conversation on their chosen topic.

courses.name: Acting 3
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description: Offers advanced acting training by exploring a variety of approaches useful in bringing the heightened dramatic texts alive on stage. Demands a free and efficient actor instrument: body, intellect, voice, and imagination simultaneously engaged and able to be compellingly present, and impeccable listening skills. Expects a significant amount of preparation, practice, and rehearsal outside the studio. Requires prior completion of basic acting training.

courses.name: Design for Immersive Performance
courses.subject: THTR
courses.description:
Covers designing space and media for live co-present collaborative storytelling, emphasizing nontraditional and immersive formats. Offers students an opportunity to develop the basic skill sets in standard programming languages and 3D visualization software of the theatrical design disciplines of lighting, projections, sound, and scenography to effectively communicate design in live and virtual space. Experience with 3D rendering/visualization software or any of the above disciplines is advantageous, though not required. Culminates in an immersive performance conceived, designed, and created by the class. Student groups create sections of the performance, focusing on a specific design discipline.

    
    
        Section information text:
        Class syllabus available in advance of registration by contacting instructor Caitlin Smith Rapoport (c.smithrapoport@northeastern.edu).

courses.name: Introduction to Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Offers an interdisciplinary course introducing key themes in gender and sexuality studies. Offers students an opportunity to learn core concepts that inform our understanding of how gender and sexuality are socially constructed and are experienced in everyday life. Drawing on women’s studies, queer studies, masculinity studies, and allied areas, the course analyzes gender, sexuality, and other dimensions of identity; explores critical issues of gender, sex, and power; and studies gendered/sexed identities in both national and transnational contexts. Topics include the gendered conceptions of love, sexuality, and violence; biological arguments about gender and sexuality; the social construction of sexuality and gender; intersections of gender, race, class, and sexuality; masculinities and femininities; theories of sexual difference; gender and the state; and gender and popular culture.

courses.name: Goddesses, Witches, Saints, and Sinners: Women and Religion
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Introduces and examines the theory that Near Eastern and European religions were originally goddess centered through analyses of image, text, and ritual in the ancient world. Explores scholarship about the patriarchalization of these primal religions. Includes a consideration of scripture such as the Hebrew Bible, Greek Testament, and Qu’ran, as well as noncanonical texts.

courses.name: Gender, Race, and Medicine
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Examines the basic tenets of “scientific objectivity” and foundational scientific ideas about race, sex, and gender and what these have meant for marginalized groups in society, particularly when they seek medical care. Introduces feminist science theories and contemporary as well as historical examples to trace the evolution of “scientific truth” and its impact on the U.S. cultural landscape. Offers students the opportunity to question assumptions about science and view the scientific process as a site for critical analysis.

courses.name: Sociology of Gender
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Considers why and how gender is socially constructed in U.S. society and looks at different theories of gender. Explores gender as an institution as well as different (cultural) expressions of masculinities and femininities. Includes topics of gender in everyday life as well as gender as an organizing principle in the institutions of families, education, workplaces, sexualities, religion, the media, politics, and forms of gender violence. SOCL 1260 and WMNS 1260 are cross-listed.

courses.name: Gender and Reproductive Justice
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Introduces the social, legal, and economic barriers to accessing reproductive healthcare domestically and internationally. Draws on various theoretical and analytic tools including critical race theory, critical legal theory, sociology of science, human rights, feminist theory, and a range of public health methods. Access to reproductive health services, including abortion, is one of the most contested political, social, cultural, and religious issues today. Covers domestic, regional, and international legal and regulatory frameworks on sexual reproductive health. HIST 2303, SOCL 2303, and WMNS 2303 are cross-listed.

courses.name: Communication and Gender
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Presents a theoretical and practical examination of the ways in which communication is gendered in a variety of contexts. Integrates into this analysis how different institutions and interpersonal situations affect our understanding of gender roles. COMM 2304 and WMNS 2304 are cross-listed.

courses.name: Black Feminist Studies
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Invites students to study the history and contemporary landscape of Black feminist scholarship. Covers a range of disciplines and historical periods to introduce students to important texts and theoretical developments in this vast and interdisciplinary field.

courses.name: Women and World Politics
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Introduces a variety of issues facing women across the globe. Focuses on the gender dynamics of key issues in international affairs. These could include economic policy, conflict and war, human rights/women’s rights, political power, and collective action. Draws on examples from various world regions since the twentieth century to analyze similarities and differences across cases around the globe. INTL 2480 and WMNS 2480 are cross-listed.

courses.name: Digital Feminisms
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Explores the unique ways that feminist activism and theory are impacted by the increasing digital nature of our world. From hashtags to Tumblr, feminists are using digital tools and platforms to aid in the pursuit of social justice. Offers students an opportunity to develop a timeline that traces feminists’ engagement with the Internet, new media, and technological innovations from the late seventies to the present. Examines the strengths and challenges that the digital world creates for feminist engagement. MSCR 2505 and WMNS 2505 are cross-listed.

courses.name: Sexual Politics and the Practice of Sexuality Education
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Uses interdisciplinarity and theory-based approaches to study the interplay between sexual politics and the fields comprising human services. Considers contemporary and historical paradigms of sexual health as they both reflect and shape politics, social inequality, cultural ideologies, and individual health and wellness. Incorporates strategies from sociology, social work, public health, and the education fields—as well as theoretical foundations from feminist, gender, queer, inequality, and prevention studies—to inform examination of social change embedded in professional practice.

courses.name: Gender, Social Justice, and Transnational Activism
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Introduces key issues, themes, and debates in feminist transnational theory, practice, and activism in contemporary contexts and how it has changed under socioeconomic, political, and cultural processes of globalization. Examines differences among women relating to race, class, sexuality, national identity, and political economy in reckoning with possibilities for sustainable social justice. Students interrogate the relationship between the local and global; the production of knowledge in different regional spaces; the pragmatics of political mobilization; the varying contours of “social justice”; and other key issues. Offers students an opportunity to discuss the impact of globalization, neoliberalism, and state and intimate violence on gendered politics and relations and to contend with the politics of difference, to debate its challenges, and to imagine possible futures for transnational gender justice.

courses.name: Gender, Crime, and Justice
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Examines the topics of femininities and masculinities and their influence on participants in the criminal justice system. Also explores topics such as gender and criminological theory; the notion of gender and offending; women and men as victims of violence; and women and men as professionals within the criminal justice system.

courses.name: Sexuality, Gender, and the Law
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description: Examines the legal regulation of gender and sexuality. Investigates concrete legal cases to study the history of constitutional interpretation and the current status of rights for women and sexual minorities. Focuses on important theoretical issues emerging in the writings of diverse feminist and queer legal scholars. Addresses debates over the value of conventional equality approaches in legal doctrine; equality vs. difference perspectives; ways in which legal language constructs gender and sexuality; the incorporation of sexuality and gender in ideologies of law; and the intersections of gender, sexuality, and race in legal doctrine and legal theory. PHIL 3500, POLS 3500, and WMNS 3500 are cross-listed.

courses.name: Feminist Resistance
courses.subject: WMNS
courses.description:
Engages students in the study of a variety of forms of feminist resistance in recent history, emphasizing the United States in the context of cross-cultural examples. Examines key feminist texts and manifestos and studies feminist activism in coalition with other social movements. Students identify and analyze unique features of gender-based activism in itself and in its intersections with other social movements, including movements and activism focused on race, class, sexuality, and physical ability.

ARCH2370.name: Islamic and Renaissance Spain
ARCH2370.description:
Covers a variety of topics in architectural history and theory. Taught by faculty according to their interests and expertise. May be repeated twice.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Between the ninth and sixteenth centuries, Spain was the site of a remarkable series of political and architectural transformations. Conquered by Muslim and Berber forces from North Africa and the Middle East and reconquered by Christian armies, it was also the center of a lively and integrated Jewish population. The architecture and landscape bear the traces of this layered political history of conflict and assimilation. The seminar will consider both first-hand accounts of the people, culture, architecture, cities and landscape of the region, as well as the mythology that has developed about the period. It will focus on Granada, Cordoba, Seville, Madrid and El Escorial. Broader questions include: What aspects of Islamic architecture and landscape in Spain distinguish it from other geographies? What is the legacy of the centuries of Muslim domination after the reconquest? What is the relationship between Spain and Italy in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries? To what extent are the hybrid terms “mudejar,” “moresco,” “mozarabic” still useful ways of describing the cultural products of Spain? What is the status of Spain in relation to the Mediterranean and to Europe?

ARCH2370.name: Topics in Architectural History
ARCH2370.description: Covers a variety of topics in architectural history and theory. Taught by faculty according to their interests and expertise. May be repeated twice.

ARCH2370.name: Topics in Architectural History

ARCH3370.name: F.L. Wright + Wasmuth Portfoli
ARCH3370.description: Covers a variety of topics in architectural history and theory in depth. Requires students to develop a research project. Topics complement the mission of the department, the college, and the university. Taught by faculty according to their interests and expertise. Please consult department for current offerings.

ARCH3370.name: Arch, War, & Climate Crisis
ARCH3370.description:
Covers a variety of topics in architectural history and theory in depth. Requires students to develop a research project. Topics complement the mission of the department, the college, and the university. Taught by faculty according to their interests and expertise. Please consult department for current offerings.
    
    
        Section information text:
        To Build is to Rebuild: Architecture, War, and the Climate Crisis 
Radical change, violent disruption, and catastrophic events, such as wars and environmental disasters, are becoming increasingly frequent and ubiquitous. Locked in a vicious circle where conflict destroys the natural environment and climate change spurs disputes over natural resources, these crises are neither marginal nor temporary: they are fundamental to global urbanization.  
This course moves beyond the illusion of designing from scratch or on a blank slate, proposing instead that to build is always to rebuild. We will examine how the dynamics of instability impact architecture and other design disciplines that are traditionally predicated on continuity, and we will investigate the agency of the built and natural environments in fostering peace or preventing conflict. 
We will explore reconstruction programs, projects, and critical frameworks from the early 20th century to the present. Through a selection of historical case studies and primary and secondary texts we will analyze the dynamics of destruction and reconstruction theoretically, historically, and spatially.

ARCH3370.name: INDIGENOUS LANDSCAPES
ARCH3370.description:
Covers a variety of topics in architectural history and theory in depth. Requires students to develop a research project. Topics complement the mission of the department, the college, and the university. Taught by faculty according to their interests and expertise. Please consult department for current offerings.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Mni Wiconi! Water is Life! Stop Line 5! Protect Oak Flat! No More Stolen Sisters! You are on Indigenous land! Starting in the present with the growing Land Back movement and ongoing struggles at Standing Rock and elsewhere, Indigenous Landscapes focuses on the Indigenous peoples of Turtle Island and their enduring and evolving relationships to land and water, and steadfast resistance to colonization and erasure. The course also highlights the work of contemporary Indigenous architects, landscape architects, planners, designers, cartographers, and artists, and considers how they are decolonizing their respective fields and more. Indigenous Landscapes features the work of scholars such as Dina Gilio-Whitaker, Nick Estes, Laura Harjo, and Robin Wall Kimmerer.

ARCH6340.name: AI in Architecture
ARCH6340.description:
Explores focused research topics relevant to the graduate program curriculum. The professor presents his or her research related to a particular urban, architectural, or technical topic. This exposes the students to methods of research and topics in current and ongoing research in the field. The students have an opportunity to engage in related and parallel research projects during the course of the semester. May be repeated without limit.
    
    
        Section information text:
        AI’s presence, which remains external to our pedagogical approach at Northeastern, has become deeply woven into the discipline of Architecture.  Its deployment has accelerated, transitioning from isolated experimental applications to integration within architectural design, theory and practice.   This course aims to provide a space for us to discuss its assimilation into our pedagogy here at Northeastern, as well as the field of architecture.  This course aims to inform, question and propose possible futures for how students may best position themselves to benefit from the full magnitude of this shift.   We will look through three complementary lenses, historical, experimental and theoretical.  Each of these offers a pedagogical perspective which we will explore AI’s architectural implications through both tangible and speculative provocations.

ARCH6340.name: Participatory Mapping
ARCH6340.description:
Explores focused research topics relevant to the graduate program curriculum. The professor presents his or her research related to a particular urban, architectural, or technical topic. This exposes the students to methods of research and topics in current and ongoing research in the field. The students have an opportunity to engage in related and parallel research projects during the course of the semester. May be repeated without limit.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This section of “Graduate Topics in Architecture” picks apart traditional conventions for delineating/remembering the shape of our physical and social geography. Students will have an opportunity to develop new and shared visual tools for mapping through experiments with meditation, sound journeys, surrealist painting, and movement practice. We will explore the power dynamics embedded in contemporary and historic cartography as a tool for stratification, oppression, and spatial injustice. Through readings and guest lectures by participatory mapping practitioners, the class will introduce students to recent efforts to democratize. Grounding texts will range from spatial practice to science fiction, including – adrienne maree brown, André Breton, Audre Lorde, Edward Soja, Guy Debord, Henri Lefebvre, Octavia Butler, Rebecca Solnit, BlackSpaceNYC, Center for Urban Pedagogy, and Center for Land Use Interpretation.
The semester will be divided into three modules:
1) ‘A’ History of Cartography;
2)Psychogeography & Surrealism;
3) Contemporary Strategies in Participatory Mapping.

ARCH6340.name: Designing Liberated Futures
ARCH6340.description:
Explores focused research topics relevant to the graduate program curriculum. The professor presents his or her research related to a particular urban, architectural, or technical topic. This exposes the students to methods of research and topics in current and ongoing research in the field. The students have an opportunity to engage in related and parallel research projects during the course of the semester. May be repeated without limit.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course focuses on the historical, socioeconomic, and legal context surrounding land. Land has been constructed as private property via processes of racialized dispossession. Property has shaped social reality, enabling the consolidation of wealth and power for some, while delimiting the arc of freedom to individualized property ownership for others.

In addition to developing a theoretical and historical understanding of this larger context, students will gain the practical tool of learning how to read case law and statutes that shape the legal context of land as commodity. While property law imposes constraints on land use (i.e., zoning law), it also provides concepts and tools for liberation (i.e., easements that allow for common use).

Understanding this context – in both constraints and possibilities – allows us to shape liberated futures based on the restoration of reciprocal and care-based relationships with the land and with all living beings. Notably, this course will examine ongoing Indigenous and houseless-led land justice movements in the Bay Area that have strategically used alternative associations and property law mechanisms to return land back to First Nations peoples and to protect new forms of communal living that have emerged from survival and self-determination.

ARCH6340.name: The Project
ARCH6340.description:
Explores focused research topics relevant to the graduate program curriculum. The professor presents his or her research related to a particular urban, architectural, or technical topic. This exposes the students to methods of research and topics in current and ongoing research in the field. The students have an opportunity to engage in related and parallel research projects during the course of the semester. May be repeated without limit.
    
    
        Section information text:
        What constitutes a “project” in contemporary architectural practice? This section treats “project” in two senses—both as a durable set of interests and preoccupations that outlast any one commission, and as a singular response to specific social, cultural, material, and disciplinary conditions. Students develop a shared vocabulary (strategies, tactics, operations) through close readings of texts, case studies, and live interviews with leading practitioners. A signature of the course is a rigorous interview pedagogy that trains students to plan, conduct, document, and interpret conversations with award-winning architects (e.g., Nader Tehrani/NADAAA; Marie Law Adams/Landing Studio). The section adopts the Journal of Architectural Education’s “Design as Scholarship” format—co-developed by the instructor—to frame design practice as scholarly knowledge production. Work culminates in a ~2,000-word final paper (or equivalent media dossier). articulating each student’s own project, supported by interview findings and case analysis.

        Section information text:
        Design has a critical role to play in promoting mental health. The scope of mental health challenges we face as a society requires innovative and comprehensive approaches that touch on every aspect of the spaces we live in, the technologies we interact with, and the information we engage with every day. Through these mediums, design has the power to both exacerbate and alleviate mental health challenges, underscoring the need for designers to develop mental health literacy. Through a combination of critical readings, case studies, and an independent project, students in this course will gain an in-depth understanding of the nature of mental health and will learn concrete principles and tools for using design to promote better mental health.

BIOT7983.name: Special Topics in Biotechnology
BIOT7983.description:
Presents selected topics of current importance in biotechnology. May be repeated five times for a maximum of 6 total semester hours.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course provides an integrated introduction to the principles and practical techniques used to isolate, cultivate, and identify microorganisms from environmental sources such as soil and water. Students will gain hands-on experience in aseptic techniques, enrichment culture, selective media, and both phenotypic and molecular identification methods. The course also covers modern DNA and sequencing technologies such as Oxford Nanopore sequencing technology platform, emphasizing their biochemical foundations, experimental design, data analysis, and applications in genomics, diagnostics, and biotechnology. Additionally, students will explore microbial fermentation strategies for environmental biotechnology, learning to design and scale processes for bioremediation. Analytical chemistry techniques will be applied to monitor pollutants and metabolites, with a focus on using instrumentation and data to optimize bioremediation outcomes. This will be held on Saturdays from 9:45 to 2 pm in the USM Science Building.

This course will give an overview of AI & ML technologies through a series of case studies, student-led projects, and hands-on interactive sessions. Some examples include applications in genomics, proteomics, metabolomics, vaccine development, antibody discovery platforms, drug delivery systems, agri-food biotechnology, clean tech biotechnology, medical diagnostics, and medical devices.

CS4973.name: Advanced Computer Systems
CS4973.description:
Offers a lecture course in computer science on a topic not regularly taught in a formal course. Topics may vary from offering to offering. May be repeated up to three times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course is an advanced version of CS 3650.  Computer Systems is
often defined as the subject that uses low-level systems concepts to
develop software that cannot otherwise be developed by a traditional
programming language.  The course goal is to quickly review the basics of
computer systems in an accelerated manner, and then use this background
to provide advanced preparation for the wealth of related systems courses
-- both at the undergraduate and M.S. level.  Examples of such systems
courses at Khoury include cybersecurity, distributed systems, operating
systems implementation, networking,  parallel computing (taught in ECE),
databases, data mining, cloud computing.  Course topics covered include
systems programming (with system calls), introduction to assembly
language, reading knowledge of the UNIX operating system, concepts
of caching (CPU cache and virtual memory/paging), shared memory and
multithreaded programming (mutex, semaphore, and condition variables),
and model checking (the principled way to determine correctness of
multithreaded programs).  The latter part of the course covers advanced
topics determined by interests of the class.  Examples include: CUDA
programming for the GPU (the core of LLMs), virtualization (e.g.,
Linux containers, lightweight virtual machines, cloud computing),
algorithms of distributed systems, wrapper libraries and interposition,
and other topics.

CS4973.description:

        Section information text:
        Abolition is a theory and practice that aims to dismantle harmful systems in society and replace them with systems that sustain human lives and livelihoods. Technology is any mechanism that people wield to effect change in our environment. In this course, we will leverage critical pedagogy and intersectional feminism to build a learning community both inside and outside of the classroom, slowly developing intentional and sustained community partnerships. From within our extended learning community, we will study and practice abolition technology: the theory and practice of dismantling harmful technologies and replacing them with technologies that sustain human lives and livelihoods.

CS6983.name: Compiling Functional Language
CS6983.description:
Offers various topics in computer science. May be repeated once.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Compiling Functional Languages: The Technology of Lambda
The class is a "second course" in compiler technology. It assumes the student has taken a first course on compilers. Thus, it assumes a basic understanding of standard compiler technology for standard programming languages of the "procedural" class, such as C: lexing, parsing, basic type checking, flow analysis, basic optimisations, instruction selection and register allocation.
The class covers the specialised technology that has been developed over the past 45 years for compiling higher-order languages based on the lambda calculus.
* Who should take the class
The course is primarily intended for young graduate students who intend to do graduate work on advanced programming languages and wish to understand the core technology of implementing these languages.
Other students may wish to learn the material for direct use in industry. (For example, the Wall Street trading firm Jane Street Capital has its own compiler group that does development on the main compiler for the functional language OCaml.)
Prerequisites are:
- A first compiler class
- Experience with functional programming languages
- A class in programming languages
- Coding skill: experience in programming sophisticated software

        This interdisciplinary and experiential special topics course explores the technical and regulatory aspects of medical device cybersecurity, focusing on the unique challenges in securing operational technology (OT) in healthcare systems—as opposed to traditional Information Technology (IT). EECE5698.name: ST: Visual Sensing & Computing
EECE5698.description:
Covers special topics in electrical and computer engineering. Topics are selected by the instructor and vary from semester to semester. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to AI-driven visual sensing and computing. Computational vision sensors play a major role in enabling machine perception in edge AI devices, and they span many scientific and engineering domains such as color science, image sensor design, optics, signal processing, and computer systems. Coverage begins with fundamental building blocks, including basic operations of digital camera systems and design/modeling of computational image sensors. Joint optimization of sensor systems and vision algorithms is introduced prior to exploring application examples related to edge machine perception. Topics covered include geometric transformations and spatial analysis, camera optics, image signal processors, image and video compression, image sensor pixel design, sensor peripheral and readout circuitry, and selected topics on sensor/algorithm co-design and in-sensor and near-sensor computing. - Concentration Course: CVLA, HSMI, MSMD

EECE5698.name: ST: Formal Mthds Dynamical Sys
EECE5698.description:
Covers special topics in electrical and computer engineering. Topics are selected by the instructor and vary from semester to semester. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: Complex dynamical systems such as robots and cyber-physical-systems consist of hardware and software which closely interact with each other. Traditionally, a closed-loop system can be rigorously designed via control theory to achieve specifications such as stability or robustness. On the other hand, complex specifications of software can be verified via formal methods. Recently, there has been a great interest in guaranteeing desired complex behaviors of dynamical systems. This course presents recent results at the intersection of formal methods and control theory for dynamical systems that combine and extend ideas from control theory, dynamical systems, automata theory, logic, and reinforcement learning. The topics include stability and reachability analysis, abstraction of dynamical systems, automata theory, various temporal logics, model checking, automata-theoretic and optimization-based control synthesis. - Concentration Course: CCSP, HSMI

EECE5698.name: ST:Superconducting Quantum Dev
EECE5698.description:
Covers special topics in electrical and computer engineering. Topics are selected by the instructor and vary from semester to semester. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: Superconducting Quantum Devices: 
This course provides an in-depth introduction to superconductor-based quantum devices, focusing on their fundamental principles, fabrication, characterization, and applications in quantum computing, sensing, and single-photon detection. Students will develop a strong foundation in superconducting materials, Josephson junctions, superconducting detectors, and circuit behavior, essential for understanding and designing superconducting quantum technologies. The course includes an introduction to basic quantum mechanics and solid-state physics concepts necessary for understanding superconducting quantum devices. It aims to launch the students towards a research or industrial career in superconductor-based quantum science and engineering. Concentration Course: MSMD, ELPO

EECE5698.name: ST: Tapeout a CMOS Chip
EECE5698.description:
Covers special topics in electrical and computer engineering. Topics are selected by the instructor and vary from semester to semester. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: This hands-on IC design course takes students from idea to a CMOS in
one semester. Students will gain experience in Cadence Virtuoso Schematic Editor, Layout
Editor, and DRC/LVS/PEX tools. Working in teams of 3–4, they will design an analog or
mixed-signal chip and complete the full tapeout flow including: (1) Concept ideation &
specification, (2) Schematic capture & pre-layout simulation, (3) Physical layout, (4)
DRC/LVS sign-off, (5) Parasitic extraction (PEX) & post-layout verification, (6) I/O
ring/padframe design & test-plan development, (7) GDSII submission to a commercial
foundry, and (8) design documentation and datasheet preparation. - Concentration Course: CCSP, MSMD, POWR

EECE5698.name: ST: Flexible & Printed Elec.
EECE5698.description:
Covers special topics in electrical and computer engineering. Topics are selected by the instructor and vary from semester to semester. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: Flexible and Printed Electronics focuses on semiconductor manufacturing using printed electronics technologies. The topics include various printing materials and functional inks, synthesis of building blocks for high quality electronic layers and their physical/optical/electronic properties, various printing technologies (inkjet, extrusion, gravure, screen, direct roll printing and contact printing) for development of passive and active devices and circuits on diverse substrates and printed electronics-based heterogenous, foil to foil and 3D integration. The students will learn how printing technologies could advance electronics manufacturing with minimal ecological footprint and greater resource-efficiency. The course also includes hands-on training showing the working of state-of-the-art printing technologies to fabricate different active and passive devices for applications such as robotics, smart interactive systems and wearables. - Concentration Course: MSMD

EECE7398.description:
Covers topics of interest to the faculty member conducting this class for advanced study. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: This class is on the special topic of large-language-model-based dialogue agents. We will cover why and where these agents are useful, what are the key capabilities of agents, how to design LLM-based dialogue agents, how these systems can influence and persuade humans, and how to deploy such systems in the real world. Students will learn about theoretical frameworks around agents and read cutting-edge agent papers. At the end of the course, students will team up, brainstorm about use cases, and develop an LLM-based dialogue agent for one application of their choice. - Concentration Course: HSMI, CVLA

EECE7398.name: ST: Legged Robots
EECE7398.description:
Covers topics of interest to the faculty member conducting this class for advanced study. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: 
The objective of this course is to present state-of-the-art legged robot technology and systematic methods for achieving stable, agile and efficient locomotion in legged machines. The course will present the emerging control theory of hybrid systems. Models of bipedal and quadrupedal robots are hybrid in nature and various phases of locomotion are modeled by ordinary differential equations interleaved with discrete transitions and reset maps. This course will make a concerted effort to help understand dynamic locomotion of point-footed walking as well as quasi-static stability criterion of flat-footed walking, e.g., zero-moment point (ZMP), capture-point (CP).  - Concentration Course: CCSP, HSMI

EECE7398.name: ST: Model-Based Deep Learning
EECE7398.description:
Covers topics of interest to the faculty member conducting this class for advanced study. May be repeated up to four times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Course Description: The course overviews the leading approaches for studying and designing model-based deep learning systems. These are methods that combine principled mathematical models with data-driven systems to benefit from the advantages of both approaches. Such model-based deep learning methods exploit both partial domain knowledge, via mathematical structures and the physics and engineering designed for specific problems, as well as learning from limited data. Students will learn how classical optimization and statistical modeling motivate neural network design, and how deep learning can be integrated with domain knowledge to create interpretable, efficient, and high performance systems. Applications include inverse problems, communications, radar, medical imaging, and dynamical systems. - Concentration Course: CCSP, CVLA, HSMI

Addresses timely trends, issues, and events. Offers students an opportunity to learn about and respond to issues of the day in an immersive, interdisciplinary format. Content and instructors vary by offering. May be repeated nineteen times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Branding, Digital Storytelling and Social Media Strategy 
Course description: Every  organization has stories worth telling, but most struggle to tell them strategically. This course bridges the gap between what you do (create transformative cultural experiences) and how you communicate that impact to the donors, patrons, and communities who sustain your mission.
You'll learn to think like a brand strategist and communications director, developing the skills to shape your organization's narrative across digital platforms. Rather than focusing on content creation techniques, this course teaches you to make strategic decisions: which stories to tell, how to position your brand, where your audiences actually are, and how to measure what matters.
Built around Kindra Hall's storytelling framework from Stories That Stick, you'll explore the four essential story types—Value, Founder, Purpose, and Customer—while developing practical expertise in social media strategy, audience engagement, and campaign design. Throughout the semester, you'll build a professional portfolio based on , creating deliverables you could present to a board or use in a job interview.
This course is designed for career-changers and working professionals who need immediately applicable skills. You don't need a marketing background—just curiosity about how brands connect with their communities and a willingness to think strategically about communication.
Textbook: Stories That Stick: How Storytelling Can Captivate Customers, Influence Audiences, and Transform Your Business by Kindra Hall (HarperCollins Leadership, 2019)

JRNL3305.name: On Ground Rptng: Asheville, NC
JRNL3305.description:
Offers specialized topics in journalism for the twenty-first century. Topic matter changes each semester. May be repeated up to eight times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Students will work from Boston and Asheville, North Carolina, to report on the state of recovery for a region that was pummeled by Hurricane Helene in September 2024 and then largely forgotten about in a fickle news cycle. For example: Residents there are still living in temporary housing while they scrape together resources to repair their vanished homes. We will also examine the broader issues and effects of such weather events (political, economical) as agencies such as the National Weather Service and FEMA have been scaled back and the very notion of climate change is under debate. Students will travel during spring break to Asheville where they will execute a variety of intermediate-level thematic topics in journalism including long-form writing, photography, video, audio and data visualization. Through interviews with local residents, business owners, activists, city officials and climate scientists, students will capture the fallout and recovery from these increasingly ferocious storms and examine why communities are not only ill-equipped but totally unprepared to deal with the coming onslaught. Additional charges to cover some of the trip will apply. This amount is yet to be determined.

JRNL3305.name: Sports Media Changng Landscape
JRNL3305.description:
Offers specialized topics in journalism for the twenty-first century. Topic matter changes each semester. May be repeated up to eight times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Students will grapple with the changing landscape of sports media and examine what the future might hold. Artificial intelligence, media rights, and consumer habits have contributed to massive changes in the field. And that doesn’t even get into the changing relationship between athletes and their fans. This class will unpack why those changes have occurred, where the industry is going, and how the shifts impact fans and the media in general. A journalism background is not required for this course.

Focuses each semester on a specific topic that is of timely relevance to journalists covering foreign affairs. Explores methods and challenges of reporting on global politics and culture, drawing on instructor expertise. Informed by current events, historical case studies, critical readings, instructor and guest lectures, and class discussions, students design original research and reporting projects in response to the course topic. Emphasizes developing skills and strategies for covering international stories, including self-directed and collaborative work in all aspects of conceiving, planning, and producing in-depth multimedia global journalism. May be repeated twice.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course examines global problems and explores why they are so intractable and the role the media plays in shaping the narrative.  Using case studies of past and current conflicts the course immerses students in different points of view, make them aware of competing narratives, and looks for solutions that can bridge seemingly intractable global challenges. 
Non Journalism majors are encouraged.

LAW7983.name: Race, Police Violence & Law
LAW7983.description:
Covers special topics in law. May be repeated up to nine times for a maximum of 30 semester hours.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This is an advanced seminar on race, policing, and the criminal justice system. We will explore the phenomenon of police violence directed at racially marginalized communities; consider historical and ongoing opposition to racialized policing; and examine police violence as an instrument of state power. We will consider community efforts to interrupt police violence and legal strategies to reduce harms caused by racialized policing. In addition to our work on race, we will consider how gender, sexual orientation, and class impact policing practices. A principal resource will be the Burnham-Nobles Digital Archive, which houses cases of lynching and other forms of historical homicidal racial violence. This Archive will ground our work in the history of racialized policing and provide a foundation upon which to examine current police operations, practices and policies.

LAW7983.name: Prac Law for a Loving World
LAW7983.description:
Covers special topics in law. May be repeated up to nine times for a maximum of 30 semester hours.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Considers the legal work needed to transition to a future society without workplace hierarchies, private wealth accumulation, and extractive land ownership – a society shaped primarily by love and cooperation, not control and violence. Focuses on development of practical skills to support worker cooperatives, ecovillages, mutual aid collectives, community-based food systems, and Indigenous land stewardship. Asks what role love plays in cooperatives and in transforming society more broadly. Explores how to nurture the conditions for love in approaches to contracts, governance, bylaws, finance, employment law, real estate, and regulation. Offers opportunities to participate in classroom simulations to envision cooperative projects, read and create cartoon legal documents, engage in reflective journaling, and gather practical tools for a transformation to a loving world.

LAW7983.name: Regulation of Asset Managers
LAW7983.description:
Covers special topics in law. May be repeated up to nine times for a maximum of 30 semester hours.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Offers students an opportunity to develop a practical understanding of the legal and regulatory framework applicable to the asset management industry. Focuses on investment advisers and investment companies and the federal legal regime that governs them, including the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, the Investment Company Act of 1940 and the rules promulgated thereunder by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Topics covered include the history of the asset management industry, current trends and issues, various matters relating to establishing, registering, operating and reorganizing investment companies, and the roles of boards of directors, investment advisers, government agencies and lawyers.

ME4699.description:
Focuses on an advanced mechanical engineering project agreed upon between the student and instructor. May be repeated without limit.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Introduces fundamental principles of high-performance road vehicle (namely cars and motorcycles) dynamics primarily through steady state kinematic analysis of vehicle geometry, motions, and interactions with the environment (road and air). Topics include tires (elastic deformation, slip angle, aligning torque, pneumatic trail); basic vehicle geometry; acceleration and braking (longitudinal weight transfer); cornering (simplified steady state stability and control, lateral load transfer, vehicle roll); suspension (spring-mass-damper system fundamentals, components, linkage kinematics); aerodynamics (relevant fluid dynamics fundamentals, wings, ground effects); and some basic driving/riding racing fundamentals.

ME7374.name: ST: Safe Control & Estimation
ME7374.description:
Offers topics of interest to the staff member conducting this class for advanced study. May be repeated without limit.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course covers/surveys topics related to the analysis, control, estimation, and optimization of various classes of uncertain control systems with safety constraints. The main theme of the course is on ensuring system safety for constrained dynamical systems in the presence of uncertainties. This course will cover various safety control topics, including control barrier functions, polyhedral/convex reachability analysis, set-valued observers, optimal/robust control and motion planning, and robust model predictive control. We will emphasize modern tools from optimization and computational geometry, as well as implementations in simulation.

MSCR3973.name: 90s Media
MSCR3973.description:

        Section information text:
        Explores 1990s media in the United States, its cultural impact, and its influence on 21st-century entertainment. Examines key examples from film, music, and television to critically analyze cultural shifts that define the 1990s, including trends related to indie cinema, “Gen X,” grunge, MTV, and the rise of the internet.

PHIL4901.name: Topics in Philosophy Seminar
PHIL4901.description:
Focuses on one specific problem or issue in philosophy. Topics vary, and students may register for the course more than once. Requires prior completion of three philosophy courses. May be repeated without limit.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Seminar in Religion: Disputers of the Way: Early Chinese Philosophy

This seminar explores in depth the native philosophical traditions of the Warring States Period (479-221 BCE) in China, focusing on the “schools” of Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, Yangism, and Legalism. The class will examine the intellectual landscape of ancient China and consider the socio-cultural factors that led to the emergence of thinkers like Confucius, Zhuangzi,and Han Feizi as well as the cultural production of texts like the Daodejing. In addition to studying the primary texts of each school, the class will also review the commentarial tradition as well as contemporary accounts in the secondary literature to understand how these schools have historically been interpreted and which philosophical themes continue to animate discussions, particularly in comparative contexts. To that end, the course will reflect on notions of the self and community, virtue, government andstatecraft, the social order, knowledge, and human flourishing among others. Most of all, we will be studying how these traditions imagined the good life or how they engaged in disputations of the Way.

PHYS7733.name: Topics: Elementary Particle Physics and Cosmology
PHYS7733.description: Covers unified theories including evidence for supersymmetric SU(5) unification of couplings, and the grand unified scale and proton decay. Discusses particle physics and cosmology including a brief introduction to Einstein’s theory of general relativity, candidates for dark matter, inflation and the primordial fluctuations, and the problem of the cosmological constant. Examines developments leading to string theory including normal mode expansion; open and closed strings; deduction of D-26 for bosonic and D-10 for superstrings; scattering amplitudes in strings; heterotic string; compactifications on the torus, orbifolds, and Calabi-Yau manifolds; 4-D strings; and superstring phenomenology. Explores physics with extra dimensions including gravity at small distances, branes, and new approaches to the hierarch problem. May be repeated without limit.

WMNS7900.name: ST: Grief, Affect, Transformtn
WMNS7900.description:
Examines selected topics in women’s, gender, and sexuality studies. May be repeated up to five times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Students must apply and be accepted to the GCWS course in order to apply. Class meets at the GCWS on MIT's campus under the instruction of Professor Chris Bobel (Umass Boston), and Professor Sarah Pinto (Tufts University). Meets Wednesdays, 5-8:20 pm. 

In this seminar, we consider the social life of grief. We are especially interested in the feminist uses and understandings of emotions related to trauma and loss, including rage, sorrow, and resignation, among a wide range of feelings.

Considering the cultural and political dynamics of what Ann Cvetkovich calls “public feelings,” we will ask, How do emotional expressions, so often assumed to be a private, personal experiences, emerge intersubjectively in gendered conditions? How might they influence social movement work and other efforts to seek justice, and how might they shape, and be shaped by forms of social belonging, exclusion, and intimacy?

WMNS7900.name: ST: Feminist & Queer Methods
WMNS7900.description:
Examines selected topics in women’s, gender, and sexuality studies. May be repeated up to five times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course meets at the GCWS on MIT's campus, Thursdays from 4:30-7:50 pm, under the instruction of Dr. Ali Erol (Boston College). Students must apply and be accepted before registering for the course. 

The purpose of doing academic research broadly revolves around knowledge production and includes steps such as hypothesizing, data coding, analyzing, connecting it to the literature, arguing with the arguments in the literature and producing charts and measuring impact and so on. Such steps usually expressed in the language borrowed from the supposedly objective natural sciences might create the impression that the way we approach knowledge production, the knowledge we produce, and the tools we use to produce knowledge with are free of political bias or they are immune from reproducing cultural or epistemic violence. Unfortunately, this is not the case.

The purpose of this course is twofold. First, we will learn to interrogate this supposedly objective process of knowledge production and the produced knowledge from the perspective of feminist and queer epistemologies and theories. Second, we will learn the ways in which we can produce knowledge based and grounded in feminist and queer epistemologies. In addition, we will practice paying close attention to locating ourselves and any research in the history of knowledge production and especially how the produced knowledge and process itself contributes to or challenges existing power structures or structures of violence in society.
